title: Introduction to Computer Science 2
body:
Introduction to Computer Science 2 is the second programming course and it rewrites the first one in C++. The problems
are the same shape as the ones in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]]. What changes is that
every type is written down, the program is translated once before it runs, and the memory a
program uses is requested and released by the person writing it.

That last change is the reason the course exists. Python holds values somewhere and never says
where. C++ makes the location visible as a number, which is a [[Pointer]], and once a program
can name a location it can build structures that grow while running. Every later computer science course
assumes this material the moment it talks about what the machine is doing.

The work splits three ways. The language is syntax, types, functions and control flow. Problem
solving is [[Algorithm|algorithms]], design documents and testing. The toolchain is ssh into a
Linux [[Shell]], editing in [[EMACS]], and compiling with `g++`, which leaves no notes behind
and takes up about half the effort.

## Topics

### Coming from Python

The same program, twice:

```python
print("hello world")
```

```cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    cout << "Hello World" << endl;
    return 0;
}
```

Six differences are visible in those five extra lines. A [[Header File]] is brought in with
`#include`, which is what `import` does in Python, and `<iostream>` is the one supplying
`cout`. Every C++ program has exactly one [[main()]], which is where execution starts, and it
is a function returning an `int`, where returning `0` reports success to whatever launched the
program. Blocks are delimited by `{` and `}`, so indentation becomes a convention that the
compiler ignores. Statements end in a semicolon. Output goes through `cout` with `<<` between
each piece. Comments are `//` to the end of a line and `/* */` across several.

The seventh difference has no visible line. C++ is [[Compiling|compiled]], so the whole file
is translated into [[Machine Language]] once, producing an executable that runs on its own.
Python is [[Interpriting|interpreted]] and translates while running. A compiled program starts
faster, runs faster, and needs recompiling after every edit. It also means a whole class of
mistake is caught before the program ever runs.

### The toolchain

The working cycle is to log in over ssh, move around the filesystem with the [[Shell]], edit
in [[EMACS]], compile, and submit. [[Workflow]] covers the routine, [[Directory]] covers
navigating, and [[Bash file]] covers scripting a repeated command.

```
g++ hello.cpp            # produces an executable called a.out
g++ hello.cpp -o hello   # names the executable hello
./hello                  # runs it
```

Never give the output the same name as the source file, because the compiler will overwrite
the source and the work is gone. [[Hardware]] and [[Processor]] cover what runs the result,
and every processor family has its own [[Machine Language]], which is why an executable built
here does not run on a different architecture. [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] in second year takes
that apart properly.

### Declaring types

A [[Variable]] in C++ is declared with a type before it is used, and the type is fixed for the
life of that name.

```cpp
int    count   = 0;        // whole number
double average = 0.0;      // number with a decimal point
char   grade   = 'A';      // one character, single quotes
bool   passed  = true;     // true or false
string name    = "Evan";   // text, double quotes
```

A [[Data type]] answers two questions at once: which values the name can hold, and how many
[[Byte|bytes]] it occupies in [[Memory]]. [[Integer]], [[Double]], [[Float]], [[Character]]
and [[Boolean]] are the built-in numeric and single-value types, and [[String]] holds text.
[[Void]] is the type of a function that returns nothing.

Types divide into two groups. An [[Atomic type]] holds one value, and a [[Compound type]]
holds many values under one name, which covers the [[Array]], the [[Structure]] and the
[[C-String]]. Textbooks call the first group atomic, primitive, built-in and fundamental
without distinction, which is why [[Primitive type]] exists as a note. [[Type casting]]
converts a value from one type to another explicitly.

Integer arithmetic behaves differently from the arithmetic in a mathematics class, because
`/` between two integers discards the remainder and `%` returns it:

```cpp
int total = 7 / 2;         // 3, the .5 is discarded
int rest  = 7 % 2;         // 1
double d  = 7 / 2.0;       // 3.5, because one operand is a double
```

That truncation is the [[Division Algorithm]] appearing as an operator, and those two
operators are what [[GCD and LCM]] and [[Prime Number]] tests are built from. How each type is
laid out in bits belongs to [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]], in [[Data representation]],
[[Integer Representation]], [[Boolean Representation]] and [[ASCII]].

### Making decisions

[[Descision]] and [[Conditional]] cover `if`, `else if` and `else`, which pick one block of
code based on a condition. The condition is an expression producing a [[Boolean]].

```cpp
if (mark >= 80) {
    grade = 'A';
} else if (mark >= 70) {
    grade = 'B';
} else {
    grade = 'C';
}
```

The branches are tested in order and the first true one runs, so their ordering is part of the
logic. [[Switch]] handles a long chain of comparisons against one value, and a `case` without
a `break` falls through into the next case, which is a bug most of the time and occasionally
deliberate. [[Dangling else]] is the trap that appears when the braces are left off a nested
`if`, because the `else` attaches to the nearest unmatched `if` and the indentation suggesting
otherwise means nothing to the compiler. [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] gives that problem
its formal name, an ambiguous grammar.

### Repeating work

[[Repetition]] covers the three loop forms. A [[While loop]] and a [[For loop]] test the
condition before running the body, so a body can run zero times. A [[Do while loop]] tests
afterwards, so its body always runs at least once.

```cpp
int total = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    total += i;            // total ends at 15
}
```

The `for` header holds the three parts every loop needs in one line: initialise the
[[Control variable]], test it, and update it. A `while` loop scatters the same three parts
across the function, and omitting the update produces an [[Infinite loop]].

```cpp
int total = 0, value;
while (cin >> value) {     // stops at end of input
    total += value;
}
```

A [[Counted loop]] knows its iteration count in advance and a [[Sentinel]] loop runs until a
marker value appears, with `cin.eof()` as the version used when reading a file.
[[Finite loop]] and [[Accumulator]] cover the remaining patterns, where an accumulator is the
running total `total` holds above. [[Loop design]] is the checklist for building one, and
[[Nested loop]] covers a loop inside a loop, where each needs its own [[Index]] variable.

### Functions

A [[Function]] is a named block of code with a declared return type and declared parameter
types. It returns at most one value.

```cpp
int area(int width, int height) {
    return width * height;
}
```

C++ requires a function to be declared before it is called, and the declaration can be
separated from the body. The declaration alone is a prototype, giving the return type, the
name and the parameter types, and it is what goes in a [[Header File]] so that other files can
call the function without seeing how it works:

```cpp
int area(int width, int height);   // prototype, note the semicolon
```

Calling a function requires no knowledge of how it works, which is procedural abstraction and
the same instinct that produces an [[Abstract Data Type]] one level up. The names in the
prototype are the [[Formal parameter|formal parameters]], the values the caller supplies are
the [[Actual parameter|actual parameters]], and [[Parameter]] covers the general idea.
[[Library]] covers what `#include` brings in, and [[main()]] is the function the operating
system calls to start the program.

### Designing a program out of functions

Polya's four steps are understand, plan, implement, evaluate, and the [[Algorithm]] is the
plan written down. An algorithm has to be ordered, explicit, effective, complete and finite.
The design documents each ask a different question about the same program. A
[[Structure chart]] asks how the functions divide the problem, an [[IPO Diagram]] asks what
goes in and comes out of each one, and [[Program design]], [[Function design]] and
[[Loop design]] cover the procedure at three scales. This is
[[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] in miniature, four semesters early.

Testing splits by direction. Top-down testing starts at [[main()]] with empty stubs standing
in for the functions below it, so the overall flow is checked first. Bottom-up testing starts
at the leaf functions, and each one needs a [[Driver]], a temporary `main()` written to call a
single function with known inputs.

### Memory, addresses and pointers

[[Memory]] is a long row of [[Byte|bytes]], each with a number identifying it, called its
[[Address]]. A variable is a name for one of those locations, and declaring it reserves enough
bytes for its type.

A [[Pointer]] is a variable whose value is an address. Two operators connect the two views:
`&x` produces the address of `x`, and `*p` produces the value stored at the address `p` holds.

```cpp
int  x = 42;
int *p = &x;               // p holds the address of x

cout << x  << endl;        // 42
cout << *p << endl;        // 42, the value at that address
*p = 99;                   // writes through the pointer
cout << x  << endl;        // 99, x changed
```

Reading `*p` is called dereferencing. One declaration trap is worth memorising:
`char *p, q;` declares one pointer and one plain `char`, because the `*` binds to the name and
not to the type.

Pointers are what make three things possible: reaching a caller's variable from inside a
function, asking for memory while the program runs, and building a structure that grows.

### Passing arguments by value and by reference

[[Call by value]] is the default. The function receives a copy of the argument, so assigning
to a parameter changes the copy and the caller's variable is untouched. [[Call by reference]]
uses `&` in the parameter declaration to pass the location, so assignment reaches the
caller's variable.

```cpp
void addOneToCopy(int n)  { n += 1; }
void addOneToCaller(int &n) { n += 1; }

int value = 5;
addOneToCopy(value);       // value is still 5
addOneToCaller(value);     // value is now 6
```

`swap()` is the standard demonstration, because a swap written with value parameters exchanges
two copies and leaves the caller's variables alone. An argument passed by reference has to be
a variable with an address, so a literal cannot be passed to a reference parameter.

### Scope and lifetime

[[Variable Scope]] is where a name is visible in the source code. [[Variable Lifetime]] is
when the storage behind it exists while the program runs. Beginners merge the two questions,
and separating them is what explains why returning a pointer to a local variable is broken.

```cpp
int *broken() {
    int local = 5;
    return &local;         // local dies when the function returns
}
```

The name `local` is visible only inside the function, and its storage is released as soon as
the function returns, so the returned address points at memory that now belongs to something
else. [[Storage Class]] is the keyword controlling both properties.

### The stack and the heap

[[Stack and Heap]] covers the two regions a program allocates from. The stack holds local
variables, is managed automatically, and gives each function call a frame that is released
when the call returns. The heap is a pool the program requests memory from explicitly, and
what it hands back stays until the program releases it.

[[Static Allocation]] fixes a size at compile time and lives on the stack.
[[Dynamic Allocation]] happens while the program runs and lives on the heap, using
[[new And delete|`new` and `delete`]].

```cpp
int n;
cin >> n;
int *scores = new int[n];  // size decided while running
// ... use scores ...
delete[] scores;           // every new needs a matching delete
```

This is why `int scores[n]` with `n` read from input fails to compile: an array's size has to
be known before the program starts. [[Dynamic Arrays]] covers the fix above. Memory obtained
with `new` and never released is a leak, and the program holds it until it exits.

### Arrays and C-strings

An [[Array]] holds many values of one type under one name, with a size fixed at compile time.
Positions are numbered from 0 to size minus one, and the position is the [[Index]].

```cpp
const int SIZE = 5;
int marks[SIZE] = {90, 75, 60, 82, 71};

cout << marks[0] << endl;  // 90
cout << marks[4] << endl;  // 71
```

Declaring a `const` for the size and using that name everywhere is what keeps the loop bounds
and the declaration in agreement. C++ performs no bounds checking, so `marks[7]` compiles and
reads whatever bytes happen to sit past the end of the array. That is the largest behavioural
difference from a [[Python List]], which raises `IndexError`.

A [[C-String]] is a `char` array ending in the null character `'\0'`, which is how a function
knows where the text stops. It therefore needs one more slot than it has characters, so
`char greeting[6] = "Hello"` holds five letters and a terminator. A [[Parallel Array]] keeps
related fields in separate arrays at matching indices, and [[Array Feild]] covers an array
stored inside a struct.

### Structures

A [[Structure]] defines a new type by grouping fields under one name, which is what parallel
arrays were approximating.

```cpp
struct Student {
    string name;
    int    mark;
};

Student s;
s.name = "Evan";
s.mark = 87;
```

The `struct` definition creates a type and no variable, so `Student s;` is what creates one.
A struct can be assigned, passed to a function and returned from one, and it is passed by
value by default, so a large struct is usually passed by reference to avoid the copy. Two
structs cannot be compared with `==`, because the compiler has no way to know which fields
matter. The struct is the direct ancestor of the [[Class]], and
[[C]] in second year re-explains it from the machine's side.

### Classes and abstract data types

An [[Abstract Data Type]] is a set of values together with the operations allowed on them,
described independently of how it is built. A stack of plates is an ADT: it holds plates,
you can push one on and pop one off, and the description says nothing about whether the plates
sit in an array or a chain of nodes.

A [[Class]] is how C++ writes an ADT down. It groups the data with the functions that operate
on it, and marks which parts the outside world can reach.

```cpp
class Counter {
private:
    int count;             // hidden from callers
public:
    Counter()      { count = 0; }
    void  bump()   { count++; }
    int   value()  { return count; }
};

Counter c;
c.bump();
c.bump();
cout << c.value() << endl; // 2
```

A function defined inside a class is a [[Method]], and one [[Object]] is a single variable of
that class type, holding its own copy of the data. [[Encapsulation]] is the bundling of the
data with its operations, and the `private` and `public` split is the information hiding that
makes the bundle worth having, since nothing outside the class can set `count` to a nonsense
value. [[Abstraction]] is the general principle, and [[Classes]] and [[Class Relationships]]
carry the mechanics.

The [[Interface]] is the promise a class makes, the [[Implementation]] is how it keeps the
promise, and the [[Client Program]] sees only the first, which is why the implementation can
be replaced without breaking anything that uses it. [[Interface Module]] is where that
separation is written down, and generalising the argument gives
[[Coupling and Cohesion]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]].

Three more mechanics arrive here. [[Overloading]] gives two functions the same name with
different parameter lists, and the compiler picks by the arguments at the call site.
[[Overriding]] is a derived class replacing a method it inherited. [[Copying]] happens on
assignment, on passing or returning by value, and at construction from an existing object,
which becomes a problem once an object holds a [[Pointer]], because copying the pointer gives
two objects one shared target. [[Javascript Objects]] and [[Object Literal]] were added later
from [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] and cover the same idea with no type declarations.

### Structures that grow

A [[Node]] is a struct holding data plus a pointer to another node of the same type. A struct
cannot contain itself, and it can contain a pointer to itself, and that single line is what
makes a growing structure possible.

```cpp
struct Node {
    int   data;
    Node *next;            // legal: a pointer to the same type
};
```

A [[Linked List]] is a chain of those, where each node points at the next and the last node's
pointer is `NULL`, marking the end. Adding an element allocates one node and adjusts two
pointers, with no copying and no fixed capacity. [[Linked Structure]],
[[Dynamic Data Structure]] and [[Data Structure]] cover the general idea, [[Singleton List]]
covers the one-element case, and [[List]] is the ADT these implement.

[[Stack]] is last in, first out, with push and pop both acting at one end, which is the plate
example above. [[Queue]] is first in, first out, with enqueue at the back and dequeue at the
front. Both are built by hand in this course and measured in
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]].

### Recursion

[[Recursion]] arrives at the end of the course. A recursive function calls itself on a smaller
version of the problem, and a base case stops the descent.

```cpp
int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;      // base case
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}
```

`factorial(4)` calls `factorial(3)`, which calls `factorial(2)`, which calls `factorial(1)`,
which returns 1, and the multiplications complete on the way back out, giving 24. It works
because every call gets its own stack frame holding its own copy of `n`, so four copies of the
function are partway through at once. A missing base case exhausts the stack, which is what a
stack overflow is. [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] takes the call stack apart in [[Subroutines]].

### Input and output

[[Input]] and [[Output]] are `cin` and `cout`. [[Buffered Input]] explains the buffer sitting
behind `cin`, which is why mixing `>>` and `getline` misbehaves: `>>` stops at the newline and
leaves it in the buffer, so the following `getline` reads that leftover newline and returns an
empty line. [[File]] covers reading and writing a file with the same operators on a stream
opened against it.

### Errors, and when each kind appears

[[Errors]] holds the taxonomy, and the three kinds differ in when they are noticed.
[[Compile Errors]] stop the build, and in C++ this includes every type mismatch, which is the
main thing the declarations buy. [[Runtime Errors]] crash the program partway through, and in
C++ the common causes are dereferencing a bad pointer and running past the end of an array.
[[Logic Errors]] are never reported: the program runs to completion and produces the wrong
answer. [[debugging]] covers working backwards from a failure to the line that caused it.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]] is the Python prequel. The same concepts
  appear there with no type declarations and no [[Memory]] management, and the distance
  between the two courses is the distance between an interpreted dynamically typed language
  and a compiled statically typed one.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] is the direct continuation, analysing [[Stack]],
  [[Queue]], [[Linked List]], [[Tree]], [[Graph]] and [[Hashing]] with [[Time Complexity]]
  to decide between them. Everything built by hand here is measured there.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] covers the same material from underneath, in
  [[Data representation]], [[Integer Representation]], [[Byte]], [[Subroutines]] for how the
  call stack works, and [[C]] as the translation layer.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] turns [[Pointer|pointers]] and [[Memory]] into
  memory-mapped hardware, where an address reaches a device.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] develops [[Interface]] and
  [[Implementation]] into [[Coupling and Cohesion]], and [[Driver]] testing into
  [[Unit testing]].
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] makes [[Stack and Heap]], [[Dynamic Allocation]] and
  [[File]] into services the kernel provides.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] revisits objects and modules with no compiler, in
  [[Javascript Objects]] and [[Node.js]].
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] supplies the number theory behind the [[Integer]] exercises:
  [[Division Algorithm]], [[GCD and LCM]], [[Prime Number]], [[Sets]] and
  [[Proof By Induction]].
